items.rationale: A reward reinforces whatever the dog is doing at the instant it arrives, not what you intended. A five-second gap is well past the roughly one-to-two-second window, so the treat landed on standing up and wandering, not on lying down.

items.answer: A marker tells the dog the exact instant it did the right thing, right before the treat arrives.
accepted: it marks the precise moment the correct behavior happened, so the dog knows what earned the reward
it is a timestamp for the correct behavior, fired the instant it happens, with the treat following
to pinpoint exactly when the dog did the right thing, since a treat alone can be too slow or vague
items.rationale: The marker's whole job is precision timing: it can be delivered the instant the right behavior happens, while handing over a treat usually takes a beat longer. An answer that only says "to tell the dog good job" misses the specific timing role and would count as partial, not correct.
Shaping only moves forward when the reward for the current step is withdrawn once the next step appears; marking the half-turn forever removes any reason for the dog to offer more.

items.answer: The dog's reliance on visible treats is a fading problem, not proof the training itself is bribery; treats need to be thinned out and swapped for other rewards over time.
accepted: it is not bribery, the treats just were never faded out, so the dog still expects to see one
the trainer skipped fading, so the behavior never became independent of a visible treat
reinforcement built the behavior correctly, but fading it down to occasional rewards was never done
items.rationale: Positive reinforcement and bribery are different mechanisms: reinforcement that never gets faded just looks like bribery from the outside. An answer that simply says "it's not bribery" without naming the fading gap would be partial.
AVSAB's position statement found reward-based methods carry the clearest advantage on both welfare and training effectiveness, explicitly with no exception made even for harder behaviors.
